Sports Car Project - Explore and Visualise Data¶

In this Notebook I will continue the Sports Car Project (dataset from Kaggle), moving onto exploring and visualising the cleaned dataset. The aim of this project is to:

  • Preview data to ensure correct loading
  • Descriptive Statistics and visualisations:
    • Single Categorical Variables: will look at the frequency counts of each category, as well as visualise this using a barchart.
    • Single Numeric Variables: will look at the central tendency (mean, median) and spread (range, IQR, standard deviation) of the numeric variables, and visualise this using histograms and boxplots.
    • One Categorical and One Numeric: will grouped the data by categories (make, engine_type and year), looking at the average per category for each numeric variable (i.e. average horsepower for combustion engines vs electric). I will visualise this on a bar chart.
  • Look at the relationship between two numeric variables using the correlation value (pearson's r) and scatterplots (i.e. is there a relationship between price and 0-60 time?).

Preview the Data¶

First I imported all the relevant modules and libraries (pandas, numpy, matplotlib and seaborn), before loading in the data (using the newly cleaned sports_car_clean.csv file created in previous notebook). I previewed the data using head(), and then looked at the data type and any missing data. The data all seems to have loaded properly, with the correct data type. The missing data was identified in the previous notebook. The only data type which will need to be changed is year, as this should be ordered categorical data rather than int64.

Categorical Variables¶

First I will look at the descriptive statistics for the categorical variables. In this dataset there are four in total, make, model, year and engine_type. I will only be calculating the descriptive statistics for make, year and engine_type, as there is a very large number of car models (over 100). While the year column does at first appear to be numeric, it doesn't behave like a continuous variable in this dataset. Therefore I will treat it like an ordered categorical variable (as noted earlier this will need to be changed as is currently int64).
For each categorical variable I will:

  • Calculate the number of unique values, and look at some examples.
  • Calculate the frequency count and proportion for each category (i.e. how many of each car make, how many of each engine type)
  • Find the mode (most frequent).
  • Visualise the frequency counts in a countplot (seaborn)

Descriptive Statistics - make¶

The car make column includes information on the car manufacturer. In this data set there are 38 different car makes, with some examples being: Porsche, Mercedes-Benz, Lamborghini and Audi.
The most common car make is Porsche, with a frequency count of 63. This accounts for nearly 10% of the cars in the dataset. Other car makes in the top five are: Audi (count: 50, percent: 8%), Mercedes-Benz (count: 46, percent: 7%), Mclaren (count: 43, percent: 7%) and Lamborghini (count: 38, percent: 6%). Some of the least common were: Ariel, Shelby, Mazda, Polestar and Ultima, each with a count of 1 (each accounting for less than 0.2% of the data).

Descriptive Statistics - engine_type¶

The engine type column is a categorical variable which includes what type of engine the car has. There are three types of engine, which are combustion, electric and hybrid. The most common engine type is a combustion engine, with a frequency count of 588. This accounts for over 92% of the cars in this dataset. Electric accounts for 7% (frequency count of 44) and hybrid accounts for less than 1% (frequency count of 4).

Descriptive Statistics - year¶

The year column represents the production year of the cars in the dataset. First step was to change the data into categorical ordered data using astype() and cat.as_ordered(). Eventhough the column appears numerical, it will be treated like an ordered categorical column from now on (i.e. using frequency count, proportion and percentage - rather than mean, median etc). There are 9 unique categories in this column, ranging from 1965 to 2023. Looking at the frequency counts and percentages, I can see that the most common year of manufactuer in this data set is 2021. Over half of the cars in this data were manufactered in this year (frequency count: 345, percentage: 54%). Next is 2022 which accounts for 39% (frequency count: 247) of the data. The other six years account for just under 7% of the data, with some years only having one car manufactered.

Numerical Variables¶

Next I will calculate the descriptive statistics for the numerical variables: 'numeric_engine_size', 'horsepower', 'torque', 'zero_to_sixty' and price columns ('price_gbp' and 'price_usd').
For each of the numerical variables I will perform the following:

  • Calculate the central tendency (mean & median) and spread (SD, range, IQR).
  • Calculate the maximum and minimum values.
  • Visualise the IQR range using a boxplot
  • Visualise the data distribution using a histogram (continuous).

Creating Descriptive Statistics Table for Numeric Data¶

I will first create a summary table containing all of the descriptive statistics for all numeric variables in this dataset. I will identify the numeric columns using select_dtypes() and then create a DataFrame which calculates the mean, median, max, min, interquartile range (IQR), range and standard deviation for our dataset. This is similar to using describe() but includes the IQR and range in the DataFrame. After this, I will go through each numeric column individually, write a short summary and visualise the distribution (histogram) and range/ interquartile range (boxplot).

In [25]:
# selects numeric columns 
numeric_df = df[[
    "numeric_engine_size",
    "horsepower",
    "torque_lb",
    "zero_to_sixty",
    "price_usd",
    "price_gbp"
]]

# calculates the IQR
def iqr(x):
    return x.quantile(0.75) - x.quantile(0.25)

# creates the summary table 
summary_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "mean": numeric_df.mean(),
    "median": numeric_df.median(),
    "max": numeric_df.max(),
    "min": numeric_df.min(),
    "IQR": numeric_df.apply(iqr),
    "range": numeric_df.max() - numeric_df.min(),
    "std_dev": numeric_df.std()
})

# displays the table 
print(summary_table.T.round(2))

Creating Functions for Boxplots and Histograms for Numeric Columns¶

I have created two functions: hist_numeric and boxplot_numeric.
The hist_numeric function takes the df and column_name as inputs, and creates a histogram displaying the distribution of the numeric column. It will also display the mean value of the data (with a red line), be titled "Histogram of the Distribution of column_name" and have approrpiately labelled x and y axis.
The boxplot_numeric function takes the df and column_name as inputs, and creates a boxplot displaying the distribution of the numeric column. It will be titled "Boxplot of the Distribution of column_name" and have appripropriately labelled x and y axis.
Both of these functions will be used on each numeric column to visually summarise the data, as well as the descriptive statistic table created above being used for a written summary.

In [26]:
# function which creates histogram for numeric variables - takes df and column name as input 


def hist_numeric(df, column_name):
    title_xlabel = column_name.replace("_", " ").title()
    mean = df[column_name].mean()
    median = df[column_name].median()
    plt.hist(df[column_name], color="lightgrey", edgecolor="black")
    plt.title(f"Histogram of the Distribution of {title_xlabel}",  fontsize=14)
    plt.axvline(mean, color="red", label=f"Mean ({mean:.2f})")
    plt.axvline(median, color="green", label=f"Median ({median:.2f})")
    plt.xlabel(title_xlabel)
    plt.ylabel("Count")
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()
In [27]:
# function which creates boxplots for numeric variables - takes df and column name as input 

def boxplot_numeric(df, column_name):
    title_ylabel = column_name.replace("_", " ").title()
    plt.boxplot(df[column_name].dropna(), patch_artist=True,
    boxprops=dict(facecolor="#DCE6F1", edgecolor="black"))
    plt.title(f"Box Plot of the Distribution of {title_ylabel}", fontsize=14)
    plt.xticks([])
    plt.ylabel(title_ylabel)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Descriptive Statistics - numeric_engine_size¶

I started with the numeric_engine_size column, which tells us in liters (L) the size of each car engine. There is a lot of missing data in this column (48 missing values), but as explained earlier it is missing not at random (MNAR), due to electric cars not having an engine size.

Descriptive Statistics

  • Values ranged from 1.50 L (BMW i8 - this is a hybrid car) to 8.40 L (Dodge Viper), which gives the engine size column a range of 6.90 L.
  • The median value was 4.00 L, while the mean was 4.45 L which suggests a slightly right skewed distribution. This is likely caused by a few large engines (6 - 8 L) which have brought the average up.
  • The Interquartile Range (IQR) was 2.50 L.
  • The standard deviation is 1.50 L, showing that most of the cars fall within 1.50 L of the mean value (around 3 L - 6 L).
  • The histogram clearly shows a cluster of cars around the 3 - 4 L region, with only a few cars with larger engines on the right. This reinforces the idea of a right skewed distribution, which was shown by the mean-median difference.
  • The boxplot shows the median is much closer to the lower quartile (around 3.5 L), compared to the upper quartile (around 6 L). There were no extreme outliers detecting for the engine size (using 1.5 IQR rule).

Descriptive Statistics - horsepower¶

The next column I looked at was the horsepower. This column tells us the power output of the car, with higher horsepower (hp) indicating higher power and performance.

Descriptive Statistics

  • The values ranged from 181 hp (Mazda MX-5 Miata) to 2000 hp (Lotus Evija), which means that the horsepower column has a range of 1819 hp.
  • The median value is 591 hp, with a mean of 626.61 hp. This suggests a slight right skewed distribution, with some very high powered cars bringing up the average.
  • The interquartile range is 261 hp
  • The standard deviation is 307 hp, which suggests that most values in the data fall within 307 hp of the mean (about 300 hp - 950 hp).
  • The histogram shows a cluster of cars around 450 - 700 hp, with only a few higher powered cars on the right hand side. This reinforces the idea of a right hand skew, which was determined from the mean-median difference.
  • The boxplot shows that the middle 50% falls roughly between 450 hp and 700 hp, with the median being close to the middle of the IQR box. There are a number of outliers on the upper end of the scale, which further supports the theory that there are a number of high powered cars which have affected the average.

The next column I looked at was the zero_to_sixty column, which tells us in seconds how quickly a car can go from 0-60 mph. It is a measure of how quick a car can accelerate from a standstill, and a lower 0-60 accelaration time generally indicates a higher performance car.

  • The boxplot shows that the middle 50% of the data falls within 3 to 4 seconds. The median is exactly in the middle of these two points at 3.50. There is two outliers towards the upper end (both with 0-60 taking over 6 seconds).

Grouping by Categories¶

Now that I have looked at the descriptive statistics for individual categorical and numerical variables, and also considered that relationships between each numerical variable (correlations, scatterplots). I will look at visualising relationships between a categorical variable and a numeric variable (e.g. average horesepower for each type of engine, average price of cars per make).

Creating Bar chart function¶

First I created a function which took df and cat_col as inputs and did the following:

  • Created a 2 X 3 subplot figure and set plot_idx to 0.
  • Iterated through a list (column_list) which contained the numeric column names.
  • It then created the title, x label and y label using the cat_col and the column names from the list. Also increased the plot_idx by one (moves onto next plot), and added a horizontal line to show overall mean.
  • make - grouped by the make (used if statement to determine) and plotted the data on a bar chart (within this it created an "Other" column for makes with a value count of less than 10).
  • engine_type and year - grouped by engine type or year (used elif statement) and plotted the data on a bar chart.
  • Hid any empty subplots (as some categories had more than others i.e. engine_type - excluded engine size as hybrid and electric engines didn't have a numeric size - just large bar for combustion).
  • displayed the plot and tidied using tight_layout().
In [38]:
def barchart(df, cat_col):

    column_list = ["horsepower", "torque_lb", "zero_to_sixty", "price_gbp", "numeric_engine_size"]
    
    # creates the subplot - fig etc 
    grid_cols = 2
    grid_rows = 3
    
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(grid_rows, grid_cols, figsize=(5*grid_cols, 5*grid_rows))
    
    axes = axes.flatten()
    
    plot_idx = 0

    # iterates through list, creates title and labels axis 
    for col in column_list:
        if cat_col == "engine_type" and col == "numeric_engine_size":
            continue
        x = cat_col.replace("_", " ").title()
        y = col.replace("_", " ").title()
        ax = axes[plot_idx]
        ax.set_title(f"Bar Chart of the Average {y} \n Grouped by {x}")
        ax.set_xlabel(x)
        ax.set_ylabel(y)
        plot_idx += 1
        ax.axhline(y=df[col].mean(), color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, label=f"Overall Mean: {df[col].mean():.2f}")


        # make plots 
        if cat_col == "make":
            new_df = df[cat_col].value_counts().reset_index()
            new_df.columns = [cat_col, "count"]
            new_df["mask"] = new_df.apply(lambda row: row[cat_col] if row["count"] > 10 else "Other", axis=1)
            group_df = df.groupby(cat_col)[col].mean().reset_index()
            merged_df = pd.merge(new_df, group_df, on=cat_col)
            ax.bar(merged_df["mask"], merged_df[col])
            ax.tick_params(axis='x', labelrotation=90)
            ax.legend()

        elif (cat_col == "year") | (cat_col == "engine_type"):
            group_df = df.groupby(cat_col, observed=True)[col].mean().reset_index()
            ax.bar(group_df[cat_col], group_df[col])
            ax.legend()
        
    # hides missing plots 
    for ax in axes[plot_idx:]:
        ax.set_visible(False)
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Grouping by Year¶

The first categorical variable I will group by is the year. I have treated the year column like a categorical variable, and have therefore grouped the data by year (i.e. calculates mean for 1965, 2022, 2023 etc). I used the function created above to display the data in a bar chart.

  • Horsepower: the bar chart for the average horsepower grouped by year shows that more recently produced cars (2014 - 2023) fall very close to the overall mean of 627.61 hp, with many being greater than the overall mean. The mean horsepower is greatest in 2023 (675.00 hp), and is lowest in 1965 (435.00). This shows that the general trend is that cars are getting more powerful each year, which makes sense as there are continous breakthroughs in technology and research in this area. However, there is one year which does not follow that pattern, which is 2020 having a very low average horsepower (462.08 hp). A quick look at the cars in 2020 show there is quite a large range of hp e.g. upper end there is Lamborghini Aventador with 770 hp, but on the other end there are five lower powered Alfa Romeos (4C Spider, 4C) with around 237 hp, which is brining the average down.

  • Torque: the bar chart for average torque grouped by year has a similar pattern to that of the horsepower (above). More recently produced cars fall very close to the overall mean of 548 lb-ft, with many being equal to or above this value. The year with the greatest average torque is 2017 (600 lb-ft) and the lowest is 2020 (386 lb-ft). While there is a general trend seems to show that cars are getting more powerful each year, there are some years which don't follow this pattern. Looking at the cars produced in 2020, again there are a large number of Alfa Romeos with a torque of around 258 lb-ft, which is brining the average for this year down.

  • 0-60 time: the bar chart for the average 0-60 time grouped by year shows that the majority of recently produced cars (2014-2023) fall very close to the overall mean of 3.55 seconds. The year with the fastest 0-60 time was 2023 (2.83 seconds) and the slowest was in 1965 (4.20 seconds). This shows that the general trend is that car acceleration is getting better each year, which reflects the previous findings of cars becoming more powerful each year (higher hp, higher torque = better acceleration). However, there is one year which doesn't follow this trend, which is again 2020 with an average 0-60 time of 3.91 seconds. This time it is the Nissan cars (Nismo - 5.2 s) which seem to be bringing the average up.

  • price: the bar chart for the average price of car (in GBP) grouped by year shows that most of the recently produced cars (2014-2023) fall close to the overall mean of 300K. The most expensive cars are from 1965 (780K) and the least expensive are from 2023 (85K). This shows that the general trend is that high performance sports cars are becoming less expensive. This makes sense as classic cars (like the Shelby Cobra - 1965) are generally much more expensive than newer produced cars. However, there is one year which does not match this pattern which is 2015, with an average of 585K. Looking at this year, there are two very expensive cars which are bringing the average price up: Lykan Hypersport (W Motor - £2.7 million) and Porsche 918 Spyder (£1.4 million). These are both limited edition high performance cars, which explains why the average price is so high for 2015.

  • engine size: the bar chart for the average engine size grouped by year shows that the majority of recently produced cars (2014-2023) fall close to the overall mean of 4.45 liters, with some years falling just below and others just above. The largest average engine size is in 2017 (8.40 liters) and the smallest is in 2022 (4.11 liters). The general trend is that engine size is decreasing over the years, with largest engines becoming less common. The year which doesn't follow this trend is 2017, with the largest engine size average of all of the years (8.40 liters). There were only three cars for the year of 2017, all of these were Dodge Vipers with a very large engine of 8.40 liters, which explains the unusually high average for this year.

Summary
The general trend is that cars are becoming more powerful each year, with the horsepower and torque increasing over time. As well as the increased power output each year, the acceleration performance of the cars are also increasing each year, with the 0-60 time decreasing over time. While the power and performance increases, the engine size seems to decrease each year, as well as the price seeming to decrease. These findings suggest that car manufacterers are finding more efficient ways to produce high powered performance sports cars, with smaller engines and with less cost. While there are some cars, especially limited editions, which don't fit this trend, the vast majority of cars are becoming more powerful, better performance and are more efficient.

Grouping by Engine Type¶

Next I grouped the data by engine type (combustion, electric and hybrid). I used the function (created above) to plot group and plot the data on bar charts. For the engine type category I excluded the numeric_engine_size column, as the only cars with a value for this column were combustion engines (i.e. there would only be one bar - plotting overall average).

  • Horsepower: the bar chart of average horsepower grouped by engine type shows that both combustion and hybrid cars fall very close to the mean of 627 hp. The electric cars have a much greater average of 1252 hp. Which shows that in terms of horsepower, the electric cars far exceeds the combustion engines and hybrids.

  • Torque: the bar chart of the average torque grouped by engine type shows that the combustion and hybrid cars are very close to the overall mean of 548 lb-ft. The electric cars have a greater average torque of 1125 lb-ft, again showing that electric far exceeds the combustion and hybrid cars.

  • 0-60: the bar chart of the average 0-60 time grouped by engine type shows combustion engines fall very close to the mean (3.64 s), with hybrids being slightly below (3.18), and electric being even lower (2.18). This shows that electric vehicles acceleration performance is better than combustion and hybrids.

  • Price: the bar chart of the average price grouped by engine type shows that both combustion and hybrid cars fall slightly below the mean of £300K. Electric cars are quite significantly above the mean, with an average of £806K. This shows that generally, electric cars are more expensive than traditional combustion engines or hybrid models.

Summary
The general trend is that electric cars are superior in power output (torque, horsepower) and performance (0-60 time), compared to traditional combustion cars or hybrids. However, they are significantly more expensive than the other types of car.

# function to view top or bottom in a list (average - by make) i.e. calculates average for each make, returns a sorted list 

def top_bottom_five(df, position, numeric_col, num):
    print("\n" + str(position.title()) + " " + str(num) + " cars based on " + str(numeric_col))
    grouped_make = df.groupby("make", observed=True)[numeric_col].mean().reset_index()
    sorted = grouped_make.sort_values(numeric_col).round(2)
    
    if position == "top":
        return sorted.tail(int(num))
    if position == "bottom":
        return sorted.head(int(num))

Grouping by Make¶

The last grouping category was the make. As there were a large number of car makes/ brands, I grouped less common car makes in an Other column (i.e. less than 10 in each group). I used the function (created earlier) to group and plot the data on bar charts.

  • Horsepower: The bar chart of the average horsepower grouped by make shows that the majority of the car makes fall near the overall mean of 627 hp, with some slightly higher and some slightly lower. The "Other" category is significantly higher than the others, with almost 2000 average hp. This shows that the cars with the highest horsepower are generally from low-volume ultra powerful car manufacterers e.g. Rimac, Pininfarina, Bugatti and Koenigsegg. The car make with the second highest average hp is Tesla, with an average horsepower of around 1000. Some of the car makes with lower horsepower are Nissan, Jaguar and Alfa Romeo.

  • Torque: The bar chart of the average torque grouped by make shows that most of the cars fall near the overall mean of 548 lb-ft. The category with the highest average torque is again the "Other" category, further supporting the idea that the cars with highest power output comes from low-volume ultra powerful car manufacterers e.g. Rimac, Bugatti etc. The second highest average torque comes from Tesla, with just over 1000 lb-ft of motor torque. Some of car makes with lower torque are Nissan, Jaguar and BMW.

  • 0-60 time: the bar chart of the average 0-60 time grouped by make shows that most of the cars fall near the overall mean of 3.55 seconds. The "Other" category has a much higher average 0-60 time compared to the rest, suggesting that there are some poorer performance cars within this category bringing the average down e.g. Mazda (6.50 s) and Subaru (4.90 s) are both contained in the other category, both having very slow acceleration from 0-60. Even though this category contains some of the fastest accelerating cars Rimac, Bugatti and Pininfarina, it still hasn't managed to bring down the average 0-60 time. The second fastest category was Tesla again, showing that it has excelled in both the power output (torque and hp) and in performance (0-60 acceleration).

  • Price: the bar chart of the average price grouped by make shows that most of the cars fall close the overall mean of £300K. The most expensive cars comes from the "Other" category, which includes low-volume luxary sports cars from brands like Rimac, Pininfarin and Pagani. The second most expensive is Lotus and then Lamboghini. There are quite a few lower priced sports car brands, like BMW, Nissan and Jaguar. a

  • Engine size the bar chart of the average engine size grouped by make shows that most cars fall close to the overall mean of 4.5 liters, with most being below the average. The "Other" category still dominates, with the average being closer to 8 liters. Some of the car makes within this category which are Shelby (Cobra - 7 liters) and Bugatti (average 8 liters). After this, the largest engine size comes from Dodge, Chevrolet and Lamboghini. The smallest engines on average are found in Alfa Romeos. There is a missing bar for Tesla's as all of these cars are electric and therefore don't have a engine size (not in liters - CC).

Summary
The highest power output (hp and torque) and performance (0-60 acceleration time) for cars are generally found in the low-volume ultra-performance brands, like Rimac, Pininfarina and Bugatti. The largest engine size is also found in some of these ultra-high performance cars like the Bugatti, but is also found in classic cars like the Shelby Cobra. These ultra-performance sports car brands are associated with much more expensive cars, which makes sense as they are the highest performance, limited edition, luxuary sports cars. :

Relationship between Numeric Variables¶

The next step is to look at the relationship between numeric variables. To do this I will look at the correlation (Pearson r) between each numeric variable, and plot the relationship on a scatter plot.
Below is a correlation matrix, showing the relationship between each numeric variable.

In [386]:

horsepower¶

  • Horsepower X Torque: there is a very strong positive correlation between hp and torque (0.94), which means that as hp increases so does the motor torque.
  • Horsepower X Price: there is a very strong positive correlation between hp and price (0.76), which means as hp increases the price increases.
  • Horsepower X Zero to Sixty: there is a very strong negative correlation between hp and 0-60 (-0.73), which means that as hp increases, the 0-60 acceleration time decreases.
  • Horsepower X engine size: there is a strong positive correlation between hp and engine size (0.61), which means that as hp increases so does the engine size, but less effect than other variables.

To summarise, there are very strong positive correlations between hp X torque and hp X price. There is a very strong negative correalation between hp X 0-60 time. And also a strong correlation between hp X engine size (less so than others).

torque_lb¶

  • Torque X horsepower: there is a very strong positive correlation between torque and horsepower (0.94), which means that as the torque increases so does the horsepower.
  • Torque X Price: there is a very strong positive correlaation between torque and price (0.75), which means as the torque increases, so does the price (in GBP).
  • Torque X zero to sixty: there is a strong negative correlation between torque and 0-60 time (-0.71), which means that as the torque increases, the 0-60 acceleration time decreases. This pattern was also seen with the horsepower (i.e. more torque and hp = car which can accelerate faster).
  • Torque X engine size: there is a moderate positive correlation between torque and engine size (0.59), which means that as torque increases, the engine size does (with moderate effect).

To summarize, there are very strong positive correlations between torque X hp and torque X price. There is a moderate positive correlation between torque X engine size, and a strong positive correlation between torque X 0-60 time.

price_gbp¶

  • Price X horsepower: there is a strong positive correlation between price and horsepower (0.76), which means that as the price increases, so does the horsepower.
  • Price X torque: there is a strong positive correlation between price and torque (0.75), which means as the price increases the torque also increases.
  • Price X 0-60 time: there is a moderate negative correlation between price and 0-60 time (-0.49), which means that as the price increases, then 0-60 time decreases with a moderate effect.
  • Price X engine size: there is a weak positive correlation between price and engine size (0.39), which means that as the price increases, so does the engine size but with only a mild effect.

To summarize, there are strong positive correlation between price X horsepower and price X torque, but only weak positive correlations between price X engine size. There is a moderate positive correlation between price X 0-60 time.

zero_to_sixty¶

  • 0-60 X horsepower: strong negative correlation between 0-60 time and horsepower (-0.73).
  • 0-60 X torque: strong negative correlation between 0-60 time and torque (-0.71).
  • 0-60 X price: moderate negative correlation between 0-60 time and price (-0.49).
  • 0-60 X engine size: moderate negative correlation between 0-60 time and engine size (-0.49).

To summarize, strong negative correlation between 0-60 X torque and 0-60 X hp, moderate negative correlations between 0-60 time X price and 0-60 time X engine size.

numeric_engine_size¶

  • engine size X horsepower: strong positive correlation between engine size and horsepower (0.61).
  • engine size X torque: moderate positive correlation between engine size and torque (0.59)
  • engine size X price: weak positive correlation between engine size and price (0.39)
  • engine size X 0-60: moderate negative correlation between engine size and 0-60 time.

To summarise, there is a strong positive correlation between engine size X horsepower, moderate positive between engine size X torque and a weak positive between engine size X price. Moderate negative correlation between engine size and 0-60 time.

Overall summary¶

All the numerical variables in the data are highly correlated with one another. The strongest correlation being between horsepower and torque (0.94), which is to be expected as both of these are measures of power output. It is also clear that these two measures of power output are associated with vehicle performance, as both are strongly associated with better acceleration (associated with lower 0-60 times). Higher power output and performance (0-60 time) is also associated with a higher price, which is again, to be expected. The variable that was least associated with the others was the engine size, with correlations being moderate-weak for most aspects. Shows that engine size may not be the best measure to determine or predict a cars performance (especially as it only includes combustion engines - electric cars do have quite high hp and torque).
There are a number of scatterplots shown below which visualise the relationships between all of these variables:

In [410]:
def scatterplot(df, column_list):
    
    # total plots
    n = len(column_list) ** 2
    
    # number of columns in figure grid
    grid_cols = 5
    grid_rows = 4
    
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(grid_rows, grid_cols, figsize=(5*grid_cols, 5*grid_rows))
    
    
    axes = axes.flatten()
    
    plot_idx = 0
    
    for y_col in column_list:      
        for x_col in column_list:
            if x_col == y_col:
                continue 
            else:
            
            
                ax = axes[plot_idx]
            
                correlation = df[x_col].corr(df[y_col])
            
                sns.regplot(x=df[x_col], y=df[y_col], scatter_kws={"color": "steelblue"}, line_kws={"color": "red"}, ci=None, ax=ax)
            
                ax.set_xlabel(x_col.replace("_", " ").title())
                ax.set_ylabel(y_col.replace("_", " ").title())
                ax.set_title(f"{y_col} vs {x_col}\nr = {correlation:.2f}")
            
                plot_idx += 1
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()




scatterplot(df, ["horsepower", "torque_lb", "zero_to_sixty", "numeric_engine_size", "price_gbp"])

Key Findings¶

  • Found that on average, electric vehicles are higher in performance (0-60 time) and power (horsepower and torque), however they are usually more expensive.
  • Found that the most powerful (horsepower and torque), high performance (0-60 time) and expensive cars comes from low-volume car brands like Rimac, Bugatti and Koenigsegg.
  • Also found that cars in general are getting more powerful, with a higher acceleration performance, however the engine size does seem to be decreasing (suggests more efficient ways of creating powerful cars).
  • The performance and power of a car are highly correlated with one another, as well as with other aspects like price and engine size. i.e. more powerful cars are typically more expensive and generally have larger engines. However, this data is correlational and so no cause can be inferred from it (i.e. I couldn't say that it is the higher horsepower of a car which causes it to be more expensive - could be the other way round, or due to another factor entirely).
